concepts: Common root of two quadratic equations
questions.question: A value of $b$ for which the equations $x^2+bx-1=0$ and $x^2+x+b=0$ have one root in common is:
questions.key_idea: Eliminate $x$ between the two equations (cross-multiplication) to get a condition on $b$ alone.
solution: Let $x$ be the common root. It satisfies $x^2+bx-1=0$ and $x^2+x+b=0$.
Treat these as two linear equations in $x^2$ and $x$ and cross-multiply: $\frac{x^2}{b^2+1}=\frac{x}{-1-b}=\frac{1}{1-b}$.
Among the options only $b=-i\sqrt3$ occurs, so the answer is (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Subtract the equations to get the common root as a linear expression in $b$, then substitute it back.
solution: Let $x$ be the common root. Subtracting the two equations kills $x^2$: $(b-1)x-(1+b)=0$.
Hence $x=\frac{b+1}{b-1}$ (here $b\neq1$; for $b=1$ the equations $x^2+x-1=0$ and $x^2+x+1=0$ have no common root).
So $b=0$ or $b=\pm i\sqrt3$; the only option is $-i\sqrt3$.
Check on option (B): $b=-i\sqrt3$ gives $x=\frac{1-i\sqrt3}{-1-i\sqrt3}=\frac{1+i\sqrt3}{2}$, and $x^2+x=\frac{-1+i\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{1+i\sqrt3}{2}=i\sqrt3$, so $x^2+x+b=0$ holds.

useful_results: Two quadratics have a common root: subtract them (or take a combination) to eliminate $x^2$; the common root is then linear, and substituting it back gives the condition.
Condition for a common root of $a_1x^2+b_1x+c_1=0$ and $a_2x^2+b_2x+c_2=0$: $(a_1c_2-a_2c_1)^2=(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)$. Here it gives $(b+1)^2=(1-b)(b^2+1)$, the same equation as above.

If two quadratics with real coefficients have a common non-real root, the conjugate is also common, so both roots are common (the equations are proportional). Here $b=\pm i\sqrt3$ is non-real, so the coefficients are not both real and only one root is shared.

concepts: Nature of roots of a real quadratic and of its composition $p(p(x))$
questions.question: The quadratic equation $p(x)=0$ with real coefficients has purely imaginary roots. Then the equation $p(p(x))=0$ has:
options: two real and two purely imaginary roots
neither real nor purely imaginary roots
questions.key_idea: A real polynomial is real on real $x$, and $ax^2+c$ is real on imaginary $x$; but $p(x)$ must equal a non-real imaginary root.
solution: Real coefficients and purely imaginary roots $\pm ik$ ($k$ real, $k\neq0$) mean the sum of the roots is $0$, so $p(x)=ax^2+c$ with $a,c$ real and $\frac ca=k^2>0$.
$p(p(x))=0$ means $p(x)$ is a root of $p$, so $p(x)=\pm ik$, i.e. $ax^2+c$ is purely imaginary.
If $x$ were real, $ax^2+c$ would be real, not $\pm ik$. So no root is real.
If $x$ were purely imaginary, $x^2$ would be real (negative), so $ax^2+c$ would again be real, not $\pm ik$. So no root is purely imaginary.
Hence the roots of $p(p(x))=0$ are neither real nor purely imaginary: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $x=u+iv$ and split $p(x)=\pm ik$ into real and imaginary parts.
solution: As before $p(x)=ax^2+c$ with $\frac ca=k^2>0$, and the roots of $p(p(x))=0$ satisfy $ax^2+c=\pm ik$ with $k\neq0$.

Equate imaginary parts: $2auv=\pm k
eq0$, so $u
eq0$ and $v
eq0$.
$u\neq0$ means $x$ is not purely imaginary, and $v\neq0$ means $x$ is not real.
This holds for every root, so no root is real or purely imaginary: option (D).
Check with $p(x)=x^2+1$: $p(p(x))=x^4+2x^2+2$, whose roots $x^2=-1\pm i$ give $x\approx\pm0.455\pm1.099i$, neither real nor purely imaginary.

useful_results: A real polynomial takes real values on $\mathbb R$, so $p(x)=r$ with $r$ non-real never has a real solution.
For an even polynomial $g(x^2)$, a purely imaginary $x$ gives a real $x^2$; so $g(x^2)$ is real on both the real and the imaginary axis, and a non-real value is attained only off both axes.
Real-coefficient quadratic with purely imaginary roots is always $a(x^2+k^2)$, i.e. $ax^2+c$ with $ac>0$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Difference of the roots of a quadratic and the range of the parameter
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all non-zero numbers $\alpha$ such that the quadratic equation $\alpha x^2-x+\alpha=0$ has two distinct real roots $x_1$ and $x_2$ satisfying the inequality $|x_1-x_2|<1$. Which of the following intervals is (are) a subset(s) of $S$?
questions.key_idea: Here $x_1x_2=1$, so $|x_1-x_2|^2=\frac1{\alpha^2}-4$; combine $|x_1-x_2|<1$ with the discriminant condition.
solution: Option (A) $\left(-\frac12,-\frac1{\sqrt5}\right)$ and option (D) $\left(\frac1{\sqrt5},\frac12\right)$ are subsets of $S$.
Options (B) and (C) contain values such as $\pm0.1$ with $|\alpha|<\frac1{\sqrt5}$, which are not in $S$. Answer: (A, D).

alternate_solutions.idea: The roots are reciprocal ($x_1x_2=1$): put them as $e^{s}$ and $e^{-s}$ and use $\cosh$ and $\sinh$.
solution: Product of roots $=1$, so the roots are $t$ and $\frac1t$. For $\alpha>0$ both roots are positive (sum $\frac1\alpha>0$), so write $t=e^{s}$, $s\neq0$ (distinct roots).
$\cosh$ is increasing in $|s|$, so $1<\cosh s<\cosh\left(\sinh^{-1}\frac12\right)=\sqrt{1+\frac14}=\frac{\sqrt5}2$ (the lower bound $1$ is strict because $s\neq0$).

For $\alpha<0$: put $x\to-x$ and multiply by $-1$; the equation becomes $(-\alpha)x^2-x+(-\alpha)=0$ with the roots negated (same difference), so $-\alpha$ must lie in $\left(\frac1{\sqrt5},\frac12\right)$, i.e. $-\frac12<\alpha<-\frac1{\sqrt5}$.
Hence $S=\left(-\frac12,-\frac1{\sqrt5}\right)\cup\left(\frac1{\sqrt5},\frac12\right)$ and the answer is (A, D).

useful_results: For $ax^2+bx+c=0$ with real roots, $|x_1-x_2|=\frac{\sqrt D}{|a|}$; so $|x_1-x_2|<k\iff D<k^2a^2$ (together with $D>0$ for distinct roots).
If $a=c$ the roots are reciprocals $t,\frac1t$, so $|x_1+x_2|>2$ for distinct real roots.
Boundary case here: $\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt5}$ gives roots $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ and $\frac1\varphi$ whose difference is exactly $1$ (golden ratio).

concepts: Power sums of the roots of a quadratic and the recurrence $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n$
questions.paragraph: Let $p,q$ be integers and let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-x-1=0$, where $\alpha\neq\beta$. For $n=0,1,2,\ldots$, let $a_n=p\alpha^n+q\beta^n$. FACT: if $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers and $a+b\sqrt5=0$, then $a=0=b$.
questions.question: If $a_4=28$, then $p+2q=$
questions.key_idea: Reduce $a_4$ to $3a_1+2a_0$ by the recurrence, then split into rational and $\sqrt5$ parts and use the FACT.
solution: Collect the $\sqrt5$ part: $\left(\frac{3p}2-\frac{3q}2\right)\sqrt5$. By the FACT, $\frac{3p}2-\frac{3q}2=0$ ... (ii).

alternate_solutions.idea: Conjugation $\sqrt5\to-\sqrt5$ swaps $\alpha,\beta$ and fixes the rational number $28$, so $p=q$ without any splitting.
solution: $\alpha^4=\frac{7+3\sqrt5}2$ and $\beta^4=\frac{7-3\sqrt5}2$, so $a_4=p\alpha^4+q\beta^4=28$ is a rational number.
Apply the conjugation $\sqrt5\mapsto-\sqrt5$ (it fixes the integers $p,q$ and the rational $28$ and swaps $\alpha^4\leftrightarrow\beta^4$): $p\beta^4+q\alpha^4=28$.

useful_results: For $a_n=p\alpha^n+q\beta^n$ with $\alpha,\beta$ the roots of $x^2-x-1=0$: $\alpha^n=F_n\alpha+F_{n-1}$ (Fibonacci), so $a_n=F_n(p\alpha+q\beta)+F_{n-1}(p+q)$. Check: $n=4$ gives $3a_1+2a_0$.
$p=q=1$ gives the Lucas numbers $L_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$ ($2,1,3,4,7,11,\ldots$); $p=-q=\frac1{\sqrt5}$ gives the Fibonacci numbers.
FACT (irrationality of $\sqrt5$): one equation $a+b\sqrt5=0$ over $\mathbb Q$ is really two equations $a=0,\ b=0$. The same holds for any $\sqrt d$ with $d$ not a perfect square.

alternate_solutions.idea: The identity must hold for every integers $p,q$; test it with $p=q=1$, where $a_n$ is the Lucas sequence.
solution: The relation asked for is the same for all integer $p,q$, so choose $p=q=1$: $a_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n=L_n$ (Lucas numbers).
Only (B) equals $322$, so the answer is (B).

useful_results: If $r_1,r_2$ are the roots of $x^2=sx+t$, then $u_n=pr_1^n+qr_2^n$ satisfies $u_{n+2}=su_{n+1}+tu_n$ for every $p,q$ (multiply $r^2=sr+t$ by $r^n$). Here $s=t=1$.
Because the relation is independent of $p,q$, any convenient choice (Lucas $p=q=1$) tests an option quickly.

concepts: Symmetric functions of the roots of two quadratic equations
questions.question: Suppose $a,b$ denote the distinct real roots of the quadratic polynomial $x^2+20x-2020$ and suppose $c,d$ denote the distinct complex roots of the quadratic polynomial $x^2-20x+2020$. Then the value of $ac(a-c)+ad(a-d)+bc(b-c)+bd(b-d)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Group the expansion as $(a^2+b^2)(c+d)-(a+b)(c^2+d^2)$; only sums and products of roots are needed.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's expansion line reads 'a^2c - ac^2 + a^2d - ad^2 + b^2c + b^2d - bd^2' and omits the term -bc^2 (the four products give eight terms). The next line, the grouping, correctly contains -c^2(a+b), so this is only a copying slip; the working and the answer 16000 are unchanged. Corrected by inserting -bc^2.
useful_results: For two pairs of roots with sums $S_a,S_c$ and products $P_a,P_c$: $\sum_{x\in\{a,b\},\,y\in\{c,d\}}xy(x-y)=S_aS_c(S_a-S_c)-2\,(S_cP_a-S_aP_c)$. Checked numerically on random integers; here it gives $(-20)(20)(-40)-2(20\cdot(-2020)-(-20)(2020))=16000-0$.
Here $S_c=-S_a$ and $P_c=-P_a$, so the second bracket vanishes and $E=S_aS_c(S_a-S_c)=16000$ at once.
Any expression symmetric in $a,b$ and in $c,d$ separately is evaluated from $a+b,\ ab,\ c+d,\ cd$; the roots (here complex $c,d$) need not be found.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Unique solution of a system of linear equations (determinant condition)
questions.question: Let $\mathbb R^2$ denote $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$. Let $S=\{(a,b,c): a,b,c\in\mathbb R$ and $ax^2+2bxy+cy^2>0$ for all $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2-\{(0,0)\}\}$. Then which of the following statements is(are) TRUE?
options: For any given $(a,b,c)\in S$, the system $ax+by=1,\ bx+cy=-1$ has a unique solution.
For any given $(a,b,c)\in S$, the system $(a+1)x+by=0,\ bx+(c+1)y=0$ has a unique solution.
questions.key_idea: $(a,b,c)\in S\iff a>0$ and $b^2<ac$; then the determinants $ac-b^2$ and $(a+1)(c+1)-b^2$ are positive.
solution: For $y\neq0$ divide by $y^2$: $a\left(\frac xy\right)^2+2b\left(\frac xy\right)+c>0$ for all real $\frac xy$, so $a>0$ and $D<0$.
Dividing by $x^2$ similarly gives $c>0$ and $D<0$. Hence $S$: $b^2<ac,\ a>0,\ c>0$.

(C) The system $ax+by=1,\ bx+cy=-1$ has a unique solution iff $\left|\begin{matrix}a&b\\b&c\end{matrix}\right|=ac-b^2\neq0$ (the PDF writes $\frac ab\neq\frac bc$). Since $b^2<ac$, this holds. (C) is correct.
(D) The system with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a+1&b\\b&c+1\end{pmatrix}$ has a unique solution iff $(a+1)(c+1)-b^2\neq0$.
$(a+1)(c+1)-b^2=(ac-b^2)+(a+c+1)$; the first bracket is positive and the second is positive, so the sum is positive and non-zero. (D) is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Positive definiteness of $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}$ as the statement $v^TMv>0$ for $v\neq0$, which gives invertibility directly.
solution: $(a,b,c)\in S$ means the symmetric matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $v^TMv>0$ for every non-zero $v=(x,y)$.
(A): $2x^2+7xy+6y^2=(2x+3y)(x+2y)$ vanishes at $(x,y)=(3,-2)\neq(0,0)$, so the form is not positive there; $\left(2,\frac72,6\right)\notin S$.
(C): if $Mv=0$ then $v^TMv=0$, which forces $v=0$. So $M$ is invertible and $Mv=(1,-1)^T$ has exactly one solution.
(D): $v^T(M+I)v=v^TMv+|v|^2>0$ for $v\neq0$, so $M+I$ is also positive definite, hence invertible; $(M+I)v=0$ has only the solution $v=0$, which is unique.
Hence (B), (C), (D) are true and (A) is false.

useful_results: $ax^2+2bxy+cy^2>0$ for all $(x,y)\neq(0,0)$ $\iff a>0$ and $ac-b^2>0$ (then $c>0$ automatically).
If $M$ is positive definite, so is $M+\lambda I$ for every $\lambda\ge0$; positive definite matrices are always invertible (all eigenvalues positive).
A real quadratic form that factors into two real linear factors, such as $(2x+3y)(x+2y)$, takes the value $0$ at a non-zero point and is never positive definite.

concepts: Roots of a polynomial and of its derivative; Vieta's relations
questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+c$ be a polynomial with real coefficients such that $f(1)=-9$. Suppose that $i\sqrt3$ is a root of the equation $4x^3+3ax^2+2bx=0$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. If $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$ and $\alpha_4$ are all the roots of the equation $f(x)=0$, then $|\alpha_1|^2+|\alpha_2|^2+|\alpha_3|^2+|\alpha_4|^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The cubic is $f'(x)=x(4x^2+3ax+2b)$; its non-real root $i\sqrt3$ forces $-i\sqrt3$ too, which fixes $a$ and $b$.
solution: $4x^3+3ax^2+2bx=x\left(4x^2+3ax+2b\right)=0$, and $i\sqrt3\neq0$ is a root of the quadratic factor $4x^2+3ax+2b$.
The coefficients are real, so the quadratic's roots are $i\sqrt3$ and $-i\sqrt3$.
Sum of roots: $-\frac{3a}4=0\Rightarrow a=0$. Product of roots: $\frac{2b}4=3\Rightarrow b=6$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rebuild $f'$ from its three roots $0,\pm i\sqrt3$, integrate, and use $|x|^2=|x^2|$ for an even quartic.
solution: Comparing coefficients: $3a=0$ and $2b=12$, so $a=0,\ b=6$ and $f(x)=x^4+6x^2+c$.
$f$ is a function of $t=x^2$: $t^2+6t-16=0\Rightarrow t=2$ or $t=-8$.
For every root $x$ we have $|x|^2=|x^2|=|t|$, and each value of $t$ comes from two roots $\pm\sqrt t$.

useful_results: If all roots of $f'$ are known, $f$ is determined up to an additive constant: $f=\int f'$.
For an even polynomial $g(x^2)$ with roots $t_j$ of $g$, the roots of $g(x^2)$ are $\pm\sqrt{t_j}$ and $|x|^2=|t_j|$, so $\sum|\alpha|^2=2\sum|t_j|$.
$\sum|\alpha|^2$ equals $\sum\alpha^2$ only if all roots are real; here Vieta gives $\sum\alpha^2=a^2-2b=-12$, but $\sum|\alpha|^2=20$.

concepts: Change of base and power rules of logarithms
questions.question: Let $a=3\sqrt2$ and $b=\frac1{5^{1/6}\sqrt6}$. If $x,y\in\mathbb R$ such that $3x+2y=\log_a\left(18\right)^{5/4}$ and $2x-y=\log_b\left(\sqrt{1080}\right)$, then $4x+5y$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Write $18=a^2$ and $\sqrt{1080}=b^{-3}$; the logarithms become the numbers $\frac52$ and $-3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Express the target $4x+5y$ as a combination of the two given forms, so $x$ and $y$ are never found.

useful_results: $\log_{A^m}\left(B^n\right)=\frac nm\log_AB$; recognise the arguments as powers of the base ($18=a^2$, $1080=5\cdot6^3=b^{-6}$) before computing anything.

When the quantity asked is linear in the unknowns, write it as a combination of the given linear forms and avoid solving for each unknown (possible exactly when the coefficient vectors are independent).
Reciprocal base: $\log_{1/b}N=-\log_bN$.
